pillar_reactions.evidence: Delivered first and tailored well to the medical context — the rep led with stiffness rather than strength ('what we're going to be focusing on is your mobility... you have those back stiffness, hips are stiff'), sized it against his fatigue ('you're coming back from radiotherapy, you're a little bit tired, you need to rest, but all you need is like 30 to 40 minutes, three to four times a week'), and promised bespoke mobility work for his weak points. He closed the pillar with a proper check: 'Does this sound like an approach that you've been looking for?' Bruno answered 'Yeah, 100%, yeah' and nothing further. Scored accepted rather than enthusiastic because the agreement was emphatic but bare — no elaboration, no question, no tie back to his own goal. The unaddressed gap: the pillar never touched whether ballistic loaded work is appropriate for someone eight weeks post-craniotomy and mid-radiotherapy, which is the one thing that would have made this pillar specific to him.

The rep pre-conceded it — 'you already have it dialed in because you're doing keto. And actually, it's very similar to what Trevor is coaching' — then delivered the standard three-variable structure (what, when, how much; clean whole foods; a 10-to-8-hour eating window). Bruno's response was flat agreement: 'It's good, yeah. It sounds good.' Scored accepted. The reaction is not the interesting part of this row; the content is. The rep then added the standard weekly balance day — 'once a week, you're going to have like a, quote unquote, like a day off... you can have a pizza or something like that, just for mind's sound' — to a man running strict ketosis for eight weeks as part of a cancer protocol, where a pizza breaks the diet outright. Bruno did not object, so nothing corrected it. Also note the live nutrition problem the pillar failed to pick up: 'sometimes I go play and I haven't ate enough. So I go and I feel like I need a little bit of a boost of energy' — a real peri-workout fuelling question on keto, raised in discovery and never answered.

The rep opened it on the prospect's own ground — 'you're a coach, so you probably understand how coaching important is' — and framed it against the treatment ahead: 'you're probably going to be going through difficult times, too, because of the treatment. But you have Trevor in your corner.' Delivered direct WhatsApp access, an instruction to over-communicate, and program adjustment when sleep or stress goes off. Bruno's in-pillar response was minimal ('Make sense? Yes'), but he volunteered the enthusiasm later, unprompted, when the money-aside question was put to him: '100% have someone to coach me, especially fitness-wise, which is gonna be something really important to me right now... It would be huge, because then I have guidance. I mean, well, work as a coach, so I know how easy... Having someone next to you to guide you through the movements and what I'm doing right, what I'm doing wrong, and have the training set up and everything, it makes it way easier. Way easier.' That is a positive reaction tied directly to his own situation and his own professional knowledge, which is the enthusiastic bar. Accountability is unmistakably the pillar that sold this prospect.

anchors.raw: I'm not Australian resident. So I'm paying everything privately. I'm paying, like, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and those things cost a fortune. So all my savings are going through cancer sheets, and doctors, and blood exams, and MRIs, and supplements.
anchors.note: The dominant anchor of the call and the reason it did not close. Privately funded oncology in Australia as a non-resident is a competing claim on the same savings account, it is already in flight, and it is unarguably higher priority than kettlebell coaching. Any $6,000 sits next to it. This is not a value objection — the value question came back at 100% — it is pure competition for a finite and shrinking pool.

anchors.raw: the amount of money that we're going to have to pay for the chemo, we are not really sure yet of the exams, how often we're going to have to do blood tests. So it's hard to commit for, like, big investments when you have something like I do.
anchors.note: Distinct from the anchor above and more damaging, because it cannot be answered with a payment plan alone. The prospect does not know the size of the bill he is budgeting against, so no amount of financial discovery produces a number. It argues for a small first instalment or a refundable deposit that holds the price, neither of which was offered.

anchors.raw: I wasn't aware of the price at all. don't know, it was, like, thousands and thousands of dollars.
anchors.note: Process finding rather than a prospect problem: the price was never pre-framed anywhere upstream. The enquiry came in through the girlfriend, and neither party arrived with any expectation of the order of magnitude. A prospect meeting $6,000 cold, twenty-four minutes into a call, in the middle of cancer treatment, was always going to defer. Whoever booked this call did not set the number.

anchors.raw: No, I'm not working right now. I got back to work yesterday actually, but I'm working just a little bit, just doing a few private lessons here and there.
anchors.note: Income is essentially zero and will remain suppressed through twelve months of chemotherapy. The purchase would come entirely out of a depleting savings balance with no replenishment, which is the structural reason a monthly instalment plan is weaker here than it would normally be.

anchors.raw: Actually, was my girlfriend that got in touch with you guys, because... we had a little while looking for what to do, like training-wise.
anchors.note: Genuinely supportive and under-used. The partner sought Primal Instinct out, had been researching training options for a while, and Bruno believes she is fully behind it — 'Yeah, she would be, for sure, 100%.' She is also the one who 'takes care of the bills'. So the person holding the chequebook is the person who wanted this, which is the strongest asset in the deal, and she was asleep on the couch and never joined the call. The rep did ask her to join, which was right, and then accepted the relay.

anchors.raw: I used to even travel with a kettlebell... I used to pay a lot on the airline fee, but it was still worth it.
anchors.note: Demonstrated willingness to pay real money for kettlebell training specifically, in a form most people would not — repeated airline excess baggage fees. He also already owns a kettlebell and swings 25 kg. The modality needs no selling, only the coaching layer does, and this anchor was never referenced back when price came up.

anchors.raw: I do it through the oxygen chamber, and then a sauna, and then I keep up with my day... Yeah, I got like a mini sauna to put on my apartment.
anchors.note: Daily hyperbaric oxygen sessions and a home sauna he bought and installed. This is a prospect who already spends discretionary money on physical recovery infrastructure, which contradicts a pure cannot-afford reading and supports the rep's should-versus-how reframe. It went unnoticed on the call and would be the strongest evidence to bring to the follow-up.

unmet_demand.want: Written payment options he could take to the person who controls the money — 'if you can send me maybe a few options of how can we pay it or if there is payment plan.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep confirmed the company has no productised plans: 'we don't have, like, a set payment plans. We always work around what's, like, in a particular case of each individual.' Nothing was sent and no numbers were named, so the prospect went into the finance conversation with his girlfriend holding a single undifferentiated figure of $6,000 USD. The capability plainly exists — the rep had already offered to 'maybe split it' — it simply is not packaged, priced or sendable.

unmet_demand.want: Assurance that loaded kettlebell training is medically safe for him — eight weeks post-craniotomy, at session 18 of 33 radiotherapy sessions, with twelve months of chemotherapy to follow.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Neither party raised it. There is no clinical screening step in the process, no requirement for clearance from an oncologist, surgeon or physio, and no medical supervision component in the offer. The programme was presented as universally applicable — 'you're going to pick up a kettlebell wherever you are, and you're going to know what to do' — with no caveat. Whether the offer can serve this prospect safely is genuinely unknown to everyone involved, including the rep, and that is the finding.

unmet_demand.want: A nutrition approach that holds his therapeutic ketogenic protocol fixed rather than overlaying the standard structure on it, including the weekly off-day.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The pillar as scripted prescribes a weekly balance day with foods that break ketosis ('you can have a pizza or something like that'). The programme could obviously just not do that, so this is not a capability limit — it is a script with no branch for a medically motivated diet, delivered verbatim to someone whose diet is part of a cancer strategy.

unmet_demand.want: A short, urgent pre-chemotherapy block — 'build a bit of core, a bit of mobility, build a bit of muscles in these next two months that I have to do it before I start chemo because it will be important.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The stated need has a hard two-month horizon set by his treatment calendar, and the offer starts at six months. The rep did not bridge the two — he did not reframe the six-month tier as covering the prehab window plus the first months of chemo, and did not offer a start date timed to the four-week gap between radiotherapy and chemo that Bruno explicitly identified as his push window ('four weeks of nothing, which is that when I'm going to boost my body as much as I can').
